sites.name: Galena Creek rock glacier
sites.coordNote: Approximate; not yet taken from a primary source
sites.label: established
sites.labelNote: Papers in 2020 and 2026. The 2026 paper treats Galena Creek as one of two Earth analogs for Martian debris-covered glaciers.
sites.role: Lead Mars story: the only pair where the same quantity, ice purity, has been estimated on both worlds.
sites.claim: Both are bodies of nearly pure ice buried under a thin layer of rock debris.

figures.q: How pure the buried ice is
figures.earthNote: Estimated from the speed of radar waves through the glacier, with an assumed value for the rock debris
figures.otherNote: Orbital radar survey. Applies to the aprons the radar could see through, which is most of them

figures.earthNote: Upper section; 2 to 3 m lower down. Drone radar later found means of 0.8 m and 1.3 m in two parts
figures.otherNote: We found no checked figure for Mars

matches.t: Galena Creek carries rock debris 1 to 1.5 m thick on its upper section and 2 to 3 m lower down, over ice estimated at 80 to 95% pure.
Orbital radar shows that the Martian debris aprons it could see through, the majority, are more than 80% water ice.
A 2026 paper tested drone radar on Galena Creek as one of two Earth analogs for Martian debris-covered glaciers, and measured the debris layer from the air.
In a survey of Mars's northern mid-latitudes, the plains of Arcadia and the glaciers of Deuteronilus Mensae meet the most criteria for accessible buried ice.

breaks.t: The Earth figure is an estimate from radar wave speed. It rests on an assumed value for the rock debris, not on a direct measurement in that study.
Debris thickness on Mars is not verified, and that thickness decides how reachable the water is.
Scale: one glacier 1.6 km long against debris aprons surveyed across a whole region.
Wyoming is far warmer, has liquid water in summer, and has life.
Terrain was not measured for this pair. The open Mars elevation grid is too coarse to resolve a 1.6 km glacier.

sites.helps: Drone radar at Galena Creek measured the debris layer from the air. On Mars, that thickness decides how reachable the water is for a crew.
sites.data: Published radar and glaciology; no terrain run

terrain: Not measured: the open Mars grid is too coarse for a 1.6 km glacier
temp: Warmer, with liquid water in summer
ice: Ice under 1 to 1.5 m of debris, estimated 80 to 95% pure from radar
sub: Buried ice body sounded by radar
ops: Radar method for finding drillable ice

sites.name: Umm Jirsan lava tube
sites.label: hypothesis
sites.labelNote: Our proposal. No study of it as a lunar-pit analog was found, and no measurement tests it.
sites.claim: A large, dry lava tube that could stand in for a lunar pit. Nobody has measured whether it does.

figures.earth: 8 to 12 m high, up to 45 m wide
figures.earthNote: Typical height and maximum width, over 1,481 m of passage
figures.otherNote: The inner pit is about 100 by 88 m across

figures.earthNote: The site paper gives none, and none was found elsewhere
figures.otherNote: A model result for the permanently shadowed part, not a measurement

matches.t: 1,481 m of passage, typically 8 to 12 m high and up to 45 m wide, in three segments split by two collapses.
A dry area: under 100 mm of rain a year.
A model of lunar pits gives a nearly constant temperature of about 290 K, about 17 °C, in the permanent shadow beyond the opening.

breaks.t: Scale: the lunar pit is 105 m deep; the tube is typically 8 to 12 m high.
No interior temperature or humidity has been published for Umm Jirsan, so the property that makes a lunar pit useful is untested here.
The steady temperature inside a lunar pit is a model result, not a measurement.
The site paper is archaeology. It has no Moon or Mars content.

sites.helps: Testing skylight entry, cave mapping and radio relay, and measuring how well the tube buffers temperature.
sites.prior: None found as a lunar-pit analog, including in three further searches on 15 November. A 2026 review frames Saudi volcanic fields as analogs for icy moons, so the claim of novelty is only this narrow.
sites.data: The 2024 survey paper; NASA on lunar pits

geo: Basalt tube; the lunar pit is in mare basalt
sub: Proposed by us as a lunar-pit analog. Tube typically 8 to 12 m high; the pit is 105 m deep
ops: Proposed: cave access, mapping and radio relay tests

sites.name: Bodélé Depression
sites.target: Dust lifting on Mars (a process, no single place)
sites.label: hypothesis
sites.labelNote: Our proposal, and a narrow one: Bodélé for dust lifting. The area is already a published Mars analog for other processes.
sites.claim: One depression that supplies about half the Saharan dust reaching the Amazon, proposed here as a test bed for how dust is lifted on Mars.

matches.t: About half of the dust carried each year from the Sahara to the Amazon basin comes from this one depression.
It emits dust on about 40% of winter days.
Mountains funnel the wind across it.
Field observations indicate the dust forms as flakes of diatomite wear each other down.

breaks.t: The dust is diatomite, the remains of diatoms: it comes from life.
How dust lifting differs in Mars's thin air is not verified.
Novelty is narrow. Bodélé is already in the Mars literature for yardangs and dunes; only the dust-lifting pairing is ours.

sites.helps: Testing dust-emission models and storm forecasting.
sites.prior: We found no published study that uses the Bodélé Depression as an analog for dust lifting on Mars. It is not new as a Mars analog in general: the area around it has been used as an analogue for dunes carving yardangs in Becquerel crater, and dunes north-east of it were compared with dunes at Hellespontus Montes. The search could not read paywalled full texts.

geo: Its yardangs and dunes have been compared with Martian ones. The diatomite itself has no Mars counterpart
dust: Proposed by us for Mars dust lifting. On Earth it supplies about half the Saharan dust reaching the Amazon
bio: The dust itself is from water life
ops: Proposed: dust forecasting for surface operations

sites.name: Sittampundi anorthosite complex
sites.tcoordNote: Approximate pin on the ridge between Shackleton and de Gerlache, not from a primary source. The soil claim is regional
sites.label: established
sites.labelNote: Established as a source of simulant. Unstudied as a field site.
sites.claim: The rock matches the composition of lunar highland soil. Nothing else about the place does.

matches.t: ISRO's lunar soil simulant LSS-ISAC-1 was produced from anorthosite of the Sittampundi complex, and is reported to resemble lunar highland regolith.
The simulant's chemistry, mineralogy and mechanical properties are reported to represent Apollo 16 highland soil.
Chandrayaan-3 made 23 measurements around its landing site at 69.37° S and found the ground there primarily ferroan anorthosite.

breaks.t: The Chandrayaan-3 result is for 69.37° S, a southern high latitude. It is not a measurement at the polar landing regions.
Composition only. It says nothing about temperature, lighting or volatiles.
A tropical, vegetated, inhabited place.
No study of Sittampundi as a field analog site was found, only as a source of rock.

sites.helps: Bulk material for landing and rover tests. ISRO's requirement was around 50 tonnes of simulant.
sites.prior: Three papers on the simulant. No study of the complex as a field site was found.

geo: Simulant made from this rock resembles lunar highland regolith
dust: Crushed rock stands in for regolith in tests
ops: Bulk simulant for landing and wheel tests

sites.coordNote: Point seen in a search result only (Mindat). The 1963 paper places the complex within 77°45′ to 78°5′ E, near 11°10′ N

sites.name: Great Kobuk Sand Dunes
sites.coordNote: Approximate, near 67° N; not from a primary source
sites.label: established
sites.labelNote: One research group: a 2009 paper on dune movement and conference abstracts in 2010 and 2012.
sites.role: A process, with a satellite record behind it.
sites.claim: Cold-climate dunes studied as an Earth analog for the dunes of Mars's high latitudes.

matches.t: Researchers study the dunes as a terrestrial analog for high-latitude Martian dunes. A NASA article calls them the place most similar to Mars's north polar dune fields.
The active dunes moved about 1.15 m a year on average between 2003 and 2008. The most likely range is 0.5 to 1.5 m a year.
Most of the dune field is snow-covered for about 70% of each year.

breaks.t: Unfrozen water lies beneath the dunes' active layer. A National Park Service page says it stays liquid all year.
The site may be less useful as its permafrost warms.

sites.helps: Change detection from orbit, and mobility on frozen sand.
sites.data: Literature only; no Mars dataset chosen

temp: Snow-covered for about 70% of each year
dust: Active dunes moved about 1.15 m a year, 2003 to 2008
bio: Unfrozen water lies beneath the dunes
ops: Change detection and mobility on frozen sand

sites.tcoordNote: Centre of Olympia Undae, the north polar dune field

sites.name: Matanomadh Formation
sites.label: established
sites.labelNote: Published as a Mars analog in 2016 and 2025. The label is ours, from that record.
sites.role: On the map with its cited evidence. Not measured: no matching open mineral data was confirmed for both worlds.
sites.claim: Iron sulfates of the kind reported from Meridiani Planum, in sediments laid over basalt.

matches.t: Jarosite, with or without gypsum, occurs in weathered Deccan basalts and the overlying Matanumadh Formation. The paper calls the setting a Martian analog.
A 2025 paper finds natrojarosite with natroalunite and kaolinite, and likens the conditions to early Mars.
An earlier abstract reports jarosite with gypsum, an association also reported from Meridiani Planum, and with goethite.

breaks.t: It is the sodium form of jarosite.
The two sources disagree on how it formed.

sites.helps: Calibrating spectral and X-ray instruments on mixtures of sulfates and clays.
sites.prior: A paper in 2016, a paper in 2025 and a 2014 abstract.

geo: Jarosite with gypsum, as reported from Meridiani

sites.name: Kamestastin Lake impact structure
sites.label: established
sites.labelNote: Used by space agencies: astronauts trained here in September 2021.
sites.role: The one pair with measured terrain on both worlds.
sites.claim: Alike in rock, unlike in terrain: the same anorthosite as the lunar highlands, in a crater far shallower and gentler than de Gerlache.
sites.terrainVerdict: Measured, and it does not match. On the same 80 m grid the lunar crater has many times the relief and much steeper slopes.
sites.terrainReading: Our reading, not tested here: Kamestastin has had about 36 million years of weather and holds a lake; de Gerlache has had no weather at all. The controls on the Method page show these measures capture ruggedness, not shape: they cannot tell a crater from a dune field.

matches.t: An impact crater about 28 km across, formed about 36 million years ago.
It formed in a target that includes anorthosite, the dominant rock of the lunar highlands.
One of the very few impact structures with anorthosite in its target rocks.
A thesis and a conference abstract describe it as a lunar analogue site.
A Canadian and a NASA astronaut trained here from 3 to 15 September 2021.

breaks.t: Terrain, measured: the two craters do not have similar relief or slopes. See the numbers above.
A lake-filled site with water, weather and life.
Soil, temperature and lighting do not match.
The elevation model cannot see under the lake or the forest. The lake is masked out of every measure.

sites.helps: Sampling of impact rocks, traverse planning and crew geology training.
sites.prior: Not new: this is an agency training site.

geo: Formed in anorthosite, the main rock of the lunar highlands
terrain: Measured on one 80 m grid, and it does not match: de Gerlache is far deeper and steeper
temp: Subarctic; nothing like polar cold traps or low sun
ice: A lake and seasonal snow, not cold-trapped ice
dust: Soil and glacial deposits, not regolith
ops: Share of ground under the 8° landing tilt limit, measured on both. Far more of Kamestastin is gentle

sites.cmpNote: Anchor and analog wording is taken from this site's notes; it is not independently sourced.
sites.tcoordNote: The Gazetteer lists three centres; this is the first, and the one the terrain window was cut at. Diameter 32.71 km

sites.name: Lake Salda
sites.label: benchmark
sites.role: The benchmark the other pairs are held against.
sites.claim: A well-studied pair: a living carbonate lake set against the ancient lake of Jezero.

figures.earthNote: A hydrous magnesium carbonate, precipitated in a highly alkaline lake (pH above 9)
figures.otherNote: With olivine, in the northern fan, seen from orbit

figures.earthNote: About 196 m deep. From a field report; no peer-reviewed source was found for these two figures
figures.otherNote: Crater diameter in the Gazetteer. The field report gives 45 km for the lake basin

matches.t: A highly alkaline lake (pH above 9) where microbial communities precipitate hydromagnesite, a hydrous magnesium carbonate.
Jezero held a lake. Its northern fan carries Mg-rich carbonate, and a unit along the old margin may preserve carbonates precipitated near the shore.
A field report gives Lake Salda as about 196 m deep and 7 km across, in an ultramafic catchment.

breaks.t: Modern and biologically active. It cannot show long exposure, burial or the slow changes rock goes through afterwards.

sites.helps: Biosignature search strategy, and recognising deposit types.
sites.prior: Well known. Shown as a benchmark, not as a find.
sites.data: Copernicus DEM GLO-30, MGS MOLA; field literature

geo: Magnesium carbonates, as found at Jezero
terrain: Measured on one 500 m grid: similar relief, steeper and rougher at Lake Salda
bio: Living lake: tests biosignature strategy, not ancient Mars
ops: Share of ground under the 8° landing tilt limit, measured on both at 500 m

limitsHead: What no Earth site can reproduce
limits: The Moon pulls at 1.62 m/s² and Mars at 3.73 m/s². Earth pulls at 9.82 m/s² everywhere.
The Moon has essentially no atmosphere.
About 0.6 kPa at the surface of Mars, under 1% of Earth's 101.4 kPa.
Neither world has Earth's shielding. No Earth site reproduces either radiation environment.
limitsNote: Each site stands in only for the characteristics listed on its page.

negative.head: The negative result
negative.text: No natural Earth site was found that reproduces the cold, the lighting or the volatiles of the lunar south pole. At the LCROSS impact site in Cabeus crater, one of the coldest of those regions, subsurface temperatures are estimated at 38 K. The Moon candidates here match rock and caves only.

operations: Gentle ground is the share of each window with a slope under 8°, the tilt NASA's Human Landing System must tolerate for surface operations. That requirement gives no baseline and site studies apply it at about 5 m, so on our 80 m grid this is a coarse screen, not a landing-safety assessment. Ground under 8° is also under the rover limits we found (VIPER 15°).
breaks: Shape only. Gravity, vacuum, temperature, lighting and erosion all differ, and the elevation model cannot see under the lake or the forest.

p: Every page argues one thing: this place on Earth is like that place on the Moon or Mars in these ways, and unlike it in these.

Terrain and temperature are measured by us: terrain on both worlds, temperature on Earth and set against published figures. Every other dimension is shown as cited evidence, with a link to its source.

Three numbers appear, and they mean different things. Terrain similarity says how alike two terrains are. Confidence says how well a page's statements are supported. Neither is an overall score for a pair, and each is shown with its parts.

ul: Benchmark: a well-studied pair, shown for comparison. Not new.
Established: published as an analog, or used by a space agency. Not new.
Hypothesis: proposed by us. Not published as this analog and not tested. A hypothesis is never shown as a finding.
Measured: the same quantity, from data, on both worlds. Today that is terrain only.
Cited: a published source says so. The link is on the page.
Partial match: alike in kind only.
Hypothesis: our proposal, not published and not tested.
Does not match: the Earth site is known to differ from its counterpart here.
Not assessed: nobody on the team has checked. This is an allowed answer, and an empty cell is never filled by a guess.

p: Both windows are 40 km squares. Each is area-averaged onto one 80 m grid before anything is measured, because slope depends on the distance between samples: two terrains are only comparable at one resolution. Slope is computed from height differences in metres.
ul: Relief: 95th minus 5th percentile height of the unmasked cells.
Median slope and 95th percentile slope, in degrees.
Roughness: the spread of height left after removing a 5 by 5 cell (400 m) moving average.

Gentle ground: the share of unmasked cells with a slope under 8°. That is the tilt NASA's Human Landing System must tolerate for surface operations (Chavers et al. 2020; NASA Inspector General report IG-26-004). The requirement gives no baseline and site studies apply it at about 5 m, so at 80 m this is a coarse screen, not a landing-safety assessment.
Slope histogram: 2 degree bins from 0 to 40, the same bins on both sides.
p2: Earth: Copernicus DEM GLO-30, read from Microsoft Planetary Computer and reprojected to UTM zone 20N at 30 m, with the lake masked. Moon: LRO LOLA polar gridded elevation LDEM_80S_80M at 80 m, with every scale factor and offset read from the product label.

The Mars pair, Lake Salda and Jezero, uses NASA's MOLA grid, which is about 463 m. That is too coarse for 80 m, so both of its windows are 60 km squares on one 500 m grid. The two pairs' numbers cannot be compared with each other.

The measures are computed in Python and written to a file. The browser draws what is in the file and never invents or recomputes a measurement. The script checks itself on made-up terrain first: a flat plane must give zero slope, and a uniform 20 degree ramp must read as 20 degrees.

The side-by-side view has a button that lights both terrains with the Sun 1.5° above the horizon. The Moon's axis is tilted about 1.5° (NASA Moon Fact Sheet: obliquity to orbit 6.68°, orbit inclined 5.145° to the ecliptic), so at its poles the Sun stays about that low. Each slope is shaded by how it faces the Sun; shadows that one hill casts on another are not drawn.

sections.h: How temperature, wind and rain are measured
p: For each Earth site we read one year of NASA MODIS land surface temperature (the MOD11A2 product from the Terra satellite: 8-day clear-sky composites at 1 km) at the one pixel that contains the site's coordinates. The page gives the average by day and by night, and the coldest and warmest 8-day averages.

The Moon or Mars side is a published figure, not our measurement, and the page says which. So this is a second measured dataset on the Earth side only. It turns "the cold does not match" into a number: how many kelvin separate the coldest night at the site from the figure for its counterpart.

Air temperature, wind and rainfall come from NASA POWER, a 25-year climatology from the MERRA-2 reanalysis on a grid of about 50 km. A reanalysis is a reconstruction constrained by observations, not a reading taken at the site, and one grid cell is far larger than most of our sites.
Limits: one pixel is 1 km across and some site coordinates are approximate; composites with cloud are skipped; a lake pixel reads the water surface.

sections.h: The zoom view: two maps, one scale
p: On the Three worlds tab, the globes can zoom in to two maps: the Earth site beside its counterpart. Both maps are drawn on a flat grid in metres centred on the place, so a kilometre covers the same number of pixels on each. The two maps are tied to one zoom level and the scale under them is printed only while they share it.

The pictures are requested live from NASA GIBS (Blue Marble, and the Landsat composite for the year 2000) and from USGS Astrogeology (the LRO wide angle camera mosaics of the Moon and the THEMIS daytime infrared mosaic of Mars). Under the live pictures sits a saved copy of the same pictures, fetched by pipeline/prerender_maps.py, so the view works with no network. A label on each map says which one is showing.

The maps are pictures for orientation. No number on this site is read from them. Near the lunar south pole the map is polar: up is toward 0° longitude, not north. The dashed square, where there is one, is the window whose terrain we measured.
The 30-second tour plays one pair through this view. Every line it shows is a claim from this site's data file with its source, ending on where the analogy stops.

sections.h: Quick test: any place on Earth
p: In the zoom view you can click the Earth map, or type a latitude and longitude, and the site measures that place's terrain in your browser and sets it beside our measured Moon window (de Gerlache) or Mars window (Jezero). It is there so anyone can propose a site we did not think of.

It is a quick test, not our pipeline, and every number from it is labelled that way. The measures are the pipeline's own, ported line for line: relief, slope, roughness, the share of ground under 8°, and the same three-part similarity. The elevation is different: open Terrain Tiles (Mapzen, hosted on AWS Open Data, built from sources that include NASA SRTM), sampled on the target's grid, where the pipeline area-averages Copernicus DEM.

We checked it where we have pipeline values. At Lake Salda it gives 841 m of relief against the pipeline's 840 m, and a median slope of 4.0° against 4.1°. At Kamestastin it gives 226 m against 216 m, and 3.3° against 3.7°. On the Sua Pan lake bed it fails: the tiles are too coarse for ground that flat, and it reads 3.2 m of roughness where the pipeline reads 0.25 m. The result card offers the same check live.

Still water is stored perfectly flat in the tiles, so flat cells are left out, as the pipeline leaves out its lake mask. The sea floor is not masked. Beyond 80° of latitude the tiles are not used. A quick-test score is a first look at terrain only; it is never added to the atlas or to a pair's confidence.
The elevation model stores the lake surface, not the lake bed, and the top of the forest, not the ground under it. The lake is masked out of every measure.
Shape says nothing about gravity, vacuum, temperature, lighting, or what the ground is made of.

The measures should agree on terrains that are alike and separate terrains that are not. We ran the same measures on five 40 km windows: two lunar craters, Kamestastin, a dune field and a flat lake bed.
ul: Two lunar craters measure alike, as expected.
A flat lake bed is clearly different from every crater, as expected.
A dune field is not separated from Kamestastin. On these measures the Earth crater sits closer to the dunes than to either lunar crater.
p2: What that means: relief, slope and roughness describe how rugged the ground is, not what shape it has. They show that Kamestastin is far gentler than de Gerlache. They cannot show whether ground is crater-shaped. A measure of shape, such as a crater's depth against its width, is the next thing to add.

The two control windows were placed by us, not taken from a source: Sua Pan near 20.75° S, 25.95° E, and the Namib Sand Sea near 24.75° S, 15.30° E. In the Sua Pan window the notebook's lake test masked 0.4% of the cells.

p: The research behind the candidate list made 416 factual claims. Each was checked against the source it cited: 391 were supported, 23 were not and were corrected or removed, and 2 sources could not be opened.

The limits of that check: much of the evidence is abstracts and press releases, and most pages were read through a tool that returns a summary of the page, not its raw text. The source list below says how much of each source was read.

Río Tinto and Yungay were added by the team after that check. Their two papers were confirmed on 15 November, by abstract only. Coordinates, the slope limit and the Bodélé literature search were also added on 15 November; their sources carry ids starting with R, G or F.

On 15 November the numbers shown on the site were re-checked against a paper, a thesis or an agency source wherever one could be opened. The Sources table gives the kind of each source; ids starting with P or Q were added by that re-check.
ul: Galena Creek: the ice purity comes from the speed of radar waves through the glacier, not from how fast the glacier flows.
Great Kobuk: the active dunes average 1.15 m a year, not 1.3; and "most similar to Mars's polar dunes" is a NASA article's wording, not the researchers'.
Bodélé: it supplies about half the dust reaching the Amazon, not half the dust leaving the Sahara.
Lunar cold: 38 K, a modelled subsurface figure at one impact site, not a 37 K average.
Sittampundi: ISRO's requirement was around 50 tonnes of simulant, not 60 to 70; and the Chandrayaan-3 result is for 69.37° S, not the pole.
Kamestastin: "one of only two craters with anorthosite" appears only in news. A paper says "one of the very few".
Lake Salda: no peer-reviewed source was found for its depth and width. They are shown as a field report's figures.
p2: The first three of these were statements the earlier source check had passed. That check read summaries of pages; the re-check read the papers or their abstracts.

p: This site was built with an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic), directed by the team. The assistant did the literature research and the source check, drafted the text, and wrote most of the code.

An AI assistant can state a wrong fact with confidence. That is why every claim here carries a link to its source, the source list says how much of each source was actually read, and a claim with no source is marked "our reading".
No image on this site is AI-generated. The globes are NASA imagery and the terrain pictures are drawn from the elevation data.

confidenceRubric.what: How well the statements on this page are supported by sources we opened. It is not a similarity score.
confidenceRubric.own: The rubric is our own, not a published standard. It is set out on the Method tab.
confidenceRubric.planNote: Where that wording and the score differ, the score is the one that can be recounted from this page.
p: Each pair has a confidence score out of 100. It says how well the statements on that pair's page are supported by sources we opened. It is not a similarity score, and a high score does not mean two places are alike: Kamestastin scores on its evidence while its measured terrain does not match.
The score is the sum of five parts. Every part is counted from what the page records: which sources back which claims, what kind of source each one is, and how much of it was read.

p2: A hypothesis is capped at 40, whatever its parts add up to, because nobody has tested the pairing.
Bands: 75 and above is High, 55 to 74 is Medium, 35 to 54 is Low, under 35 is Very low.
The rubric rewards reading better sources. A score rises when someone opens the primary paper and records it, and falls if a claim turns out to rest on news alone.
The scores are computed by pipeline/score_confidence.py and stored in the data file. The page shows the stored numbers and their parts.

terrainSim.h: How terrain similarity is worked out
p: Where both worlds have a terrain window, the page gives a terrain similarity percentage. It is the plain average of three parts, each from 0 to 100, and it is always shown with them.
ul: Slopes: how much the two slope histograms overlap. For each 2 degree bin take the smaller of the two shares, then add them up.
Relief: the smaller relief divided by the larger.
Roughness: the smaller roughness divided by the larger.
p2: It is a plain average because we have no reason to weight one part above another. It describes terrain only. It says nothing about rock, temperature, ice or anything else, and it does not feed the confidence score.
The controls test it: the table below gives every window's similarity to de Gerlache.
